ἴδητε. ἐπαχύνθη γὰρ ἡ καρδία τοῦ λαοῦ τούτου, καὶ τοῖς ὠσὶν αὐτῶν βαρέως ἤκουσαν καὶ τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς αὐτῶν ἐκάμμυσαν, μήποτε ἴδωσιν τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς καὶ τοῖς ὠσὶν ἀκούσωσιν καὶ τῇ καρδίᾳ συνῶσιν καὶ ἐπιστρέψωσιν καὶ ἰάσομαι αὐτούς». 19.7 καὶ μεταξὺ ἄλλων ἐπιφέρει· «καὶ τὸν βασιλέα κύριον Σαβαὼθ εἶδον τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς μου. καὶ ἀπεστάλη πρὸς μὲ ἓν τῶν σεραφίμ» καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς. 19.8 Τὸν ὀφθέντα τοίνυν κύριον Σαβαὼθ καὶ βασιλέα Ἠσαΐας μὲν οὗτος αὐτὸν τὸν θεὸν πατέρα εἶναι οἶδεν. 19.9 Παῦλος δὲ ἐν τῇ βίβλῳ τῶν ἀποστολικῶν πράξεων τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα τυγχάνειν ὂν ἀπεφήνατο τοιῶσδε ἀνειπών· «καλῶς τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον ἐλάλησεν πρὸς τοὺς πατέρας ὑμῶν διὰ Ἠσαΐου τοῦ προφήτου λέγοντος· πορεύθητι πρὸς τὸν λαὸν τοῦτον καὶ εἰπὲ αὐτῷ· ἀκοῇ ἀκούσετε καὶ οὐ μὴ συνῆτε» καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς, ὡς πρόκειται. 19.10 Ἰωάννης δὲ ἐν εὐαγγελίῳ τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ θεοῦ εἶναι διωρίσατο. ἔφη γάρ· «τοσαῦτα σημεῖα πεποιηκότος τοῦ Ἰησοῦ οὐκ ἐδύναντο πιστεύειν, ὅτι εἶπεν Ἠσαΐας· τετύφλωκεν αὐτῶν τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς καὶ ἐπήρωσεν αὐτῶν τὴν καρδίαν, ἵνα μὴ ἴδωσιν τοῖς ὀφθαλμοῖς καὶ νοήσωσιν τῇ καρδίᾳ καὶ ἐπι στρέψωσιν καὶ ἰάσομαι αὐτούς». καὶ εὐθὺς ἐπάγει· «ταῦτα δὲ εἶπεν Ἠσαΐας, ὅτε εἶδεν τὴν δόξαν αὐτοῦ», τουτέστιν τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ. ταῦτα μὲν δὴ περὶ τούτων ὧδέ πῃ. 19.11 Ἄκουε δὲ καὶ ἕτερα τῆς αὐτῆς δυνάμεως, τοῦ ∆αυῒδ ἐν ψαλμῷ ϟδʹ ἐκ προσώπου τοῦ θεοῦ πατρὸς ᾄσαντος τῇ λύρᾳ τοιῶσδε· «ἐπείρασάν με οἱ 22 πατέρες ὑμῶν καὶ εἶδον τὰ ἔργα μου τεσσαράκοντα ἔτη. διὸ προσώχθισα τῇ γενεᾷ ταύτῃ καὶ εἶπον· ἀεὶ πλανῶνται τῇ καρδίᾳ. αὐτοὶ δὲ οὐκ ἔγνωσαν τὰς ὁδούς μου. ὣς ὤμοσα ἐν τῇ ὀργῇ μου· εἰ εἰσελεύσονται εἰς τὴν κατάπαυσίν μου». 19.12 Παῦλος Ἑβραίοις γράφων ἐκ τοῦ αὐτοῦ ψαλμοῦ ἀπὸ τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος διορίζεται τόνδε τὸν τρόπον· «καθὼς εἶπεν», φησίν, «τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον· σήμερον ἐὰν τῆς φωνῆς μου ἀκούσητε, μὴ σκληρύνητε τὰς καρδίας ὑμῶν, ὡς ἐν τῷ παραπικρασμῷ κατὰ τὴν ἡμέραν τοῦ πειρασμοῦ, οὗ ἐπείρασάν με οἱ πατέρες ὑμῶν καὶ εἶδον τὰ ἔργα μου τεσσαράκοντα ἔτη». 19.13 καὶ Στέφανος εἰς τὰς ἀποστολικὰς πράξεις τοὺς Ἰουδαίους ἀπὸ τῆς αὐτῆς ἐντρέπων γραφῆς ἔφη· «σκληροτράχηλοι καὶ ἀπερίτμητοι τῇ καρδίᾳ καὶ τοῖς ὠσίν, ὑμεῖς ἀεὶ τῷ πνεύματι τῷ ἁγίῳ ἀντιπίπτετε, ὡς οἱ πατέρες ὑμῶν καὶ ὑμεῖς». 19.14 Ὁμοίως δὲ ἐξ Αἰγύπτου ὡδηγηκέναι τοὺς Ἑβραίους ὁ μὲν Μωϋσῆς κύριον λέγει. ἐν τῷ δευτερονομίῳ· «κύριος γάρ», φησίν, «μόνος ἦγεν αὐτούς, καὶ
pass_a_gloss: [...] holy, Lord Sabaoth, full is the heaven and all the earth of his glory.' 19.6 And after other things he says: 'he said to me: say to the people: by hearing you will hear and by no means understand, and seeing you will see and by no means perceive. For the heart of this people was made thick, and with their ears they heard heavily, and their eyes they closed, lest ever they see with the eyes and hear with the ears and understand with the heart and turn back, and I will heal them.' 19.7 And in between other things he brings on: 'and the king, Lord Sabaoth, I saw with my eyes. And there was sent to me one of the seraphim', and the things in order after. 19.8 The Lord Sabaoth and King who was seen, then, this Isaiah knows to be the God and Father himself. 19.9 But Paul in the book of the apostolic Acts declared it to happen to be the Holy Spirit, speaking out in this way: 'well did the Holy Spirit speak to your fathers through Isaiah the prophet, saying: go to this people and say to it: by hearing you will hear and by no means understand' and the things in order after, as is set out before. 19.10 But John in the gospel defined it to be the Son of God. For he said: 'Jesus having done so many signs, they were not able to believe, because Isaiah said: he has blinded their eyes and maimed their heart, so that they not see with the eyes and understand with the heart and turn back, and I will heal them.' And at once he brings on: 'these things Isaiah said when he saw his glory', that is, of the Son of God. These things indeed about these matters thus, somehow. 19.11 And hear also other things of the same force, David in psalm 94 (LXX; English 95) from the person of God the Father having sung with the lyre in this way: 'your fathers tested me and saw my works forty years. Therefore I was vexed with this generation and said: always they wander in the heart. And they did not know my ways. As I swore in my anger: if they will enter into my rest' (oath form: they shall not enter). 19.12 Paul, writing to Hebrews from the same psalm, defines [it] as from the Holy Spirit in this manner: 'just as', he says, 'the Holy Spirit said: today if you hear my voice, do not harden your hearts, as in the embitterment, according to the day of the testing, where your fathers tested me and saw my works forty years.' 19.13 And Stephen in the apostolic Acts, shaming the Jews from the same scripture, said: 'stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always fall against the Holy Spirit, as your fathers, also you.' 19.14 And likewise Moses on his part says that the Lord has guided the Hebrews out of Egypt. In Deuteronomy: 'for the Lord', he says, 'alone led them, and [...]'
pass_b_english: … holy, Lord Sabaoth; heaven and all the earth are full of his glory” (Isaiah 6:3).

And after other things he says: “He said to me: Say to the people: Hearing you will hear and will not understand, and seeing you will see and will not perceive. For the heart of this people has grown thick, and with their ears they have heard heavily, and they have shut their eyes, lest they should see with their eyes and hear with their ears and understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them” (Isaiah 6:9-10). And in between, among other things, he adds: “And I saw with my eyes the King, the Lord Sabaoth. And one of the seraphim was sent to me” (Isaiah 6:5-6), and what follows.

Now this Isaiah knows that the Lord Sabaoth and King who was seen is God the Father himself. But Paul, in the book of the Acts of the Apostles, declared that it is the Holy Spirit, speaking out in these words: “The Holy Spirit spoke well to your fathers through Isaiah the prophet, saying: Go to this people and say to it: Hearing you will hear and will not understand” (Acts 28:25-26), and the rest, as set out above.

And John in his Gospel determined that it is the Son of God. For he said: “Though Jesus had done so many signs, they could not believe, because Isaiah said: He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, so that they should not see with their eyes and understand with their heart and turn, and I would heal them” (John 12:37-40). And at once he adds: “These things Isaiah said when he saw his glory” (John 12:41), that is, the glory of the Son of God. So much, then, more or less, on these matters.

But hear also other texts of the same force. David, in the ninety-fifth Psalm, sang on the lyre in the person of God the Father in these words: “Your fathers tested me and saw my works for forty years. Therefore I was angered with this generation and said: They always go astray in their heart; and they did not know my ways. So I swore in my anger: They shall not enter into my rest” (Psalm 95:9-11).

Paul, writing to the Hebrews from the same psalm, determines that it comes from the Holy Spirit, in this way: “As the Holy Spirit says,” he writes, “Today, if you hear my voice, do not harden your hearts as in the provocation, on the day of testing, where your fathers tested me and saw my works for forty years” (Hebrews 3:7-9). And Stephen, in the Acts of the Apostles, putting the Jews to shame from the same scripture, said: “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit; as your fathers did, so do you” (Acts 7:51).
Likewise Moses, for his part, says that it was the Lord who led the Hebrews out of Egypt. In Deuteronomy he says: “For the Lord alone led them, and …” (Deuteronomy 32:12)

choices.choice: Retranslated the whole section from the Greek. The old English turned 19.9 into 'Paul … finding the Holy Spirit to be, declared thus, interjecting' (reader report, acts/SOURCE_ISSUES.md item 10; τυγχάνειν ὂν ἀπεφήνατο … ἀνειπών = 'declared that it is the Holy Spirit, speaking out'); reversed Isaiah 6:6 ('he was sent to one of the seraphim' for ἀπεστάλη πρὸς μὲ ἓν τῶν σεραφίμ, 'one of the seraphim was sent to me'); printed the opening fragment of Isaiah 6:3 as a whole sentence; made ἐντρέπων 'threatening' and attached it to 'scripture'; rendered μόνος ἦγεν αὐτούς 'was alone with them'; read ταῦτα μὲν δὴ περὶ τούτων ὧδέ πῃ as 'These things indeed are somewhat about these matters'; and attached a reference '(Isa 6:5)' to Didymus' own sentence in 19.8. References: all abbreviations written out; Acts 28:25 widened to 28:25-26 (the quotation runs into 28:26); 'Ps 95:7-11' narrowed to Psalm 95:9-11 (Didymus quotes only LXX 94:9-11; the Greek 'ψαλμῷ ϟδʹ' is Psalm 94 in Greek numbering, 95 in English); Hebrews 3:7-8 widened to 3:7-9 (the quotation runs to 'forty years'); the reference in 19.8 removed.

choices.english: … holy, Lord Sabaoth; heaven and all the earth are full of his glory”
choices.why: The section opens inside the quotation of Isaiah 6:3 that began in the previous section (ἅγιος ἅγιος). Only the words this section holds are translated, with a leading ellipsis. Didymus' text has 'heaven and all the earth', not the LXX 'all the earth'; his wording is kept.

choices.english: And in between, among other things, he adds
choices.why: Didymus quotes Isaiah 6:9-10 first and then reaches back to 6:5-6; 'in between' keeps his note that these words stand between the passages already quoted.
Hebrew oath idiom in the LXX: 'if they shall enter' means a solemn denial.

choices.english: determines that it comes from the Holy Spirit
choices.why: Didymus' point: Hebrews names the Spirit as speaker of the psalm in which God the Father speaks, so the same words belong to Father and Spirit.
μέν sets up a contrast that the next section completes (another writer giving the same act to another Person); 'for his part' keeps the balance without adding words from the next section.
Printed page-line number 22 inside the Greek of 19.11 is page debris and is skipped; ἐπι στρέψωσιν is one word split by a line break.

choices.term: ταῦτα μὲν δὴ περὶ τούτων ὧδέ πῃ
choices.english: So much, then, more or less, on these matters
choices.why: A closing formula; πῃ is Didymus' modest hedge and is kept as 'more or less'.
